cases.title: State the claim, then show the measured spread and its limit
cases.lesson: A claim earns belief when the measurement behind it follows at once, with what was and was not measured visible on the same screen.
cases.opening: The claim alone, as one short statement with one accented word.
cases.story_arc: Claim → the measured range and what was counted → the limit of the measurement.
cases.payoff: The viewer sees the spread that supports the claim and the conditions it was measured under.

beats.spoken_idea: A scoop is not a measurement.
beats.visible: One statement on its own, the key word accented.
beats.why_this_picture: The claim is short enough to read in one glance before any evidence arrives.

beats.spoken_idea: I weighed ten scoops from the same bag. They ranged from seven to eleven grams.
beats.visible: The range lands as the hero figure; the lightest, the heaviest and the count arrive as tiles.
beats.why_this_picture: The spread is the evidence, and the tiles say exactly what was counted.

beats.spoken_idea: That is one spoon and one bag, so yours will differ. It will not be zero.
beats.visible: The same board gains a limit footer naming the spoon and the bag.
beats.why_this_picture: Putting the limit on screen stops one kitchen's numbers from reading as a universal result.

cases.title: Let both bars land before naming the difference
cases.lesson: When two measured values are compared, show both before stating the difference, then show the conditions that make the comparison fair.
cases.opening: A two-line headline asks which option is faster; no bars yet.
cases.story_arc: Question → both measured bars → the difference → the conditions both options shared.
cases.payoff: The viewer reads the difference and knows the comparison was like for like.

beats.spoken_idea: Is the new route actually faster?
beats.visible: The headline and its eyebrow, with the bar area still empty.
beats.why_this_picture: Asking before answering gives the bars a question to settle.

cases.title: Rank every part on one axis before naming the largest
cases.lesson: When a total is broken into parts, put every part on one axis first and name the largest only after the viewer can see that it is the largest.
cases.opening: The headline names the total being broken down, with a one-line key to the parts.
cases.story_arc: The hour → four parts on one axis → the verdict on the part worth fixing.
cases.payoff: The viewer sees which part is largest before the speaker says so.

beats.spoken_idea: Here is where one hour of editing goes.
beats.visible: The headline and the key, before any bar.
beats.why_this_picture: Naming the total first tells the viewer what the bars will add up to.

cases.title: Grow the checklist one row per spoken check, then mark it done
cases.lesson: A checklist the speaker walks through should gain one row per spoken check, keep earlier rows in place and end on an explicit finished state.
cases.opening: The headline says what the checklist is for.
cases.story_arc: Purpose → four checks, one per sentence → the finished state.
cases.payoff: The complete list stays readable and ends on a clear finished state.

beats.spoken_idea: Four checks before you send a quote. First, the scope in writing.
beats.visible: The headline, then the first checklist row with its badge.
beats.why_this_picture: The first row arrives with the first check, so the list and the speech stay together.
